\section{Discussion}

Verdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection: the model determines whether execution deviated from expected behavior.
Exception events are the most explicit deviation signal---self-contained diagnostic moments that explain why \texttt{exception\_only} matches or exceeds VOTA: non-exception components dilute the model's attention without providing complementary information.

The Tier~1 accuracy (${\geq}$99\%) confirms that fault indicator presence detection is sufficient.
The contribution lies in quantifying the cost of richer representations: adding trace information actively \emph{hurts} (VOTA $<$ \texttt{exception\_only}, Table~\ref{tab:ablation}), compounded by tokenizer-driven truncation on DeepSeek (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
The 6.22pp SFT advantage over the best regex concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases, confirming the model learns semantic distinctions beyond mere presence detection (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
Training dynamics reveal that DeepSeek seeds with near-identical losses differ by 8.24pp in accuracy (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}), and the 0.50pp cross-model exception gap provides a clean capability measure unconfounded by truncation (Appendix~\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}).
Irreducible error analysis is in Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}.

\paragraph{Why exception\_only outperforms ae\_only.}
Although \texttt{ae\_only} achieves 99.92\% on seed 42, it is a strict superset of the exception signal: assertion-point comparisons include the exception event (when present) plus additional information such as fallback local variable states.
Multi-seed evaluation reveals that this extra content introduces noise: \texttt{ae\_only} achieves 99.64\% mean accuracy ($\pm$0.49, seeds 42/123/456) while \texttt{exception\_only} achieves 99.83\% ($\pm$0.00).
The zero-variance result for \texttt{exception\_only} indicates that it captures a minimal sufficient signal---the compact exception event---while \texttt{ae\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) occasionally mislead the model, manifesting as seed-dependent variance ($\sigma{=}$0.49pp).
Thus \texttt{exception\_only} is both more precise and more stable than its superset.

\paragraph{SFT vs.\ regex incremental analysis.}
The gap between B5 (format marker, 99.33\%) and SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) isolates the value of learned semantic understanding (McNemar $p{=}0.041$, Table~\ref{tab:regex}).
Among 8 test samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions (from 2 distinct problems), the SFT model correctly classifies 6 (all from MBPP/113, a try/except ValueError pattern) while B5 misclassifies all 8. The 2 remaining errors (HumanEval/95, GeneratorExit) are irreducible. At the problem level, SFT handles 1/2 exception-type edge cases vs B5's 0/2.
This confirms that SFT learns a genuine semantic boundary---distinguishing caught from uncaught exceptions---rather than merely detecting exception presence or format markers.

\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}
The B5 baseline (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}) achieves 99.33\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker (\texttt{[No exception data in trace]}) present in all pass samples.
This near-ceiling performance from a trivial pattern raises a concern: does SFT also learn this shortcut?
The answer is partially yes---the format marker correlates perfectly with the pass class---but the SFT model additionally handles the 8 boundary samples where exceptions occur in passing code, achieving 6/8 correct vs.\ B5's 0/8.
A \emph{nomarker} ablation (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}) confirms genuine exception semantics: Qwen-7B 3-seed mean 97.65\%$\pm$0.96 and Qwen-1.5B 97.82\%, a drop of only ${\sim}$2pp.
The marker contribution (${\sim}$9\% of total lift) is small relative to semantic content (${\sim}$91\%), confirming that SFT learns exception semantics rather than format shortcuts.
Both signal layers are independently scale-invariant (1.5B and 7B produce equivalent nomarker accuracy).

\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}
Samples 901 and 905 (HumanEval/95, \texttt{check\_dict\_case}) are misclassified by most configurations: Qwen-7B (3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B, and CodeLlama-13B seed 42/456 all produce exactly these 2 errors.

However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
This confirms that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most initializations) rather than a hard data limitation: the representation supports perfect accuracy, though most LoRA initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
On this task, exception-only accuracy is \emph{signal-limited} rather than \emph{capacity-limited}: three architecture families spanning 1.5B to 13B converge on the same floor, while \texttt{no\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\% $\to$ 75.1\% $\to$ 76.5\%).

\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}
The two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\geq}$99\%; Tier~2 = 85.6\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.
First, it implies a \emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may actively degrade performance through attention dilution.
Second, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised---though our results show that even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces---line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior---have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
Yet a fundamental question remains: \emph{which components of an execution trace actually matter?}

\citet{wang2025dcsh} found that no single trace representation consistently outperforms others, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---is fundamentally different: it is fault detection, not generation.
Which trace components matter for this task type is unknown.

We present the first systematic study of what trace components drive verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2025coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

\textbf{Exception events alone achieve near-perfect verdict prediction across all four models: 99.83\% on Qwen-7B ($\pm$0.00, 3 seeds) and Qwen-1.5B, 99.89\% on CodeLlama-13B ($\pm$0.10, 3 seeds; one seed reaches 100\%), and 99.33\% on DeepSeek (2/3 seeds; 1 outlier at 91.09\%).}
VOTA degrades by 14.96pp on DeepSeek (confounded by tokenizer-driven truncation; 91.7\% of DeepSeek training samples were affected).
We approximately decompose the full-trace-to-VOTA gap into gradient dilution (${\sim}$26\%) and information overload (${\sim}$74\%), suggesting that irrelevant trace content is the primary bottleneck.
The novelty: (1)~adding trace information actively \emph{hurts}, (2)~we approximately decompose \emph{why} into a ${\sim}$26/74 split, and (3)~the cross-model gap is confounded by truncation (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Scale-invariant exception signal}: Exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.83\% across four models (1.5B--13B, three families), while \texttt{no\_trace} shows 9.19pp scale sensitivity (67.3--76.5\%); cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) yields 100\%, and a format-marker ablation confirms ${\sim}$91\% of the signal is semantic (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:nomarker}, \S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
\item \textbf{Information density decomposition}: The full-trace-to-VOTA gap approximately splits into gradient dilution (${\sim}$26\%) and information overload (${\sim}$74\%) (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertions) achieve ${\geq}$99\%; Tier~2 (loops) reaches 85.6\% (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}

Verdict prediction is fundamentally fault detection: the model determines whether execution deviated from expected behavior.
Exception events are the most explicit deviation signal---self-contained diagnostic moments that explain why \texttt{exception\_only} matches or exceeds VOTA: non-exception components dilute the model's attention without providing complementary information.

The Tier~1 accuracy (${\geq}$99\%) confirms that fault indicator presence detection is sufficient.
The contribution lies in quantifying the cost of richer representations: adding trace information actively \emph{hurts} (VOTA $<$ \texttt{exception\_only}, Table~\ref{tab:ablation}), compounded by tokenizer-driven truncation on DeepSeek (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
The 6.22pp SFT advantage over the best regex concentrates on caught-exception boundary cases, confirming the model learns semantic distinctions beyond mere presence detection (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}).
Training dynamics reveal that DeepSeek seeds with near-identical losses differ by 8.24pp in accuracy (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}), and the 0.56pp cross-model exception gap provides a clean capability measure unconfounded by truncation (Appendix~\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}).
Irreducible error analysis is in Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}.

\paragraph{Why exception\_only outperforms ae\_only.}
Although \texttt{ae\_only} achieves 99.92\% on seed 42, it is a strict superset of the exception signal: assertion-point comparisons include the exception event (when present) plus additional information such as fallback local variable states.
Multi-seed evaluation reveals that this extra content introduces noise: \texttt{ae\_only} achieves 99.64\% mean accuracy ($\pm$0.49, seeds 42/123/456) while \texttt{exception\_only} achieves 99.83\% ($\pm$0.00).
The zero-variance result for \texttt{exception\_only} indicates that it captures a minimal sufficient signal---the compact exception event---while \texttt{ae\_only}'s additional components (fallback locals, assertion formatting) occasionally mislead the model, manifesting as seed-dependent variance ($\sigma{=}$0.49pp).
Thus \texttt{exception\_only} is both more precise and more stable than its superset.

\paragraph{SFT vs.\ regex incremental analysis.}
The gap between B5 (format marker, 99.33\%) and SFT \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) isolates the value of learned semantic understanding (McNemar $p{=}0.041$, Table~\ref{tab:regex}).
Among 8 test samples where pass-labeled code triggers exceptions (from 2 distinct problems), the SFT model correctly classifies 6 (all from MBPP/113, a try/except ValueError pattern) while B5 misclassifies all 8. The 2 remaining errors (HumanEval/95, GeneratorExit) are misclassified by most training configurations (see Appendix~\ref{sec:irreducible}). At the problem level, SFT handles 1/2 exception-type edge cases vs B5's 0/2.
This confirms that SFT learns a genuine semantic boundary---distinguishing caught from uncaught exceptions---rather than merely detecting exception presence or format markers.

\paragraph{Format marker sensitivity.}
The B5 baseline (Appendix~\ref{sec:regex_baselines}) achieves 99.33\% by exploiting a deterministic format marker (\texttt{[No exception data in trace]}) present in all pass samples.
This near-ceiling performance from a trivial pattern raises a concern: does SFT also learn this shortcut?
The answer is partially yes---the format marker correlates perfectly with the pass class---but the SFT model additionally handles the 8 boundary samples where exceptions occur in passing code, achieving 6/8 correct vs.\ B5's 0/8.
A \emph{nomarker} ablation (\S\ref{sec:nomarker}) confirms genuine exception semantics: Qwen-7B 3-seed mean 97.65\%$\pm$0.96 and Qwen-1.5B 97.82\%, a drop of only ${\sim}$2pp.
The marker contribution (${\sim}$9\% of total lift) is small relative to semantic content (${\sim}$91\%), confirming that SFT learns exception semantics rather than format shortcuts.
Both signal layers show comparable accuracy across the two tested scales (1.5B and 7B produce 97.8\% and 97.7\% nomarker accuracy, respectively).

\paragraph{Near-perfect floor, not hard ceiling.}
Samples 901 and 905 (HumanEval/95, \texttt{check\_dict\_case}) are misclassified by most configurations: Qwen-7B (3 seeds), Qwen-1.5B, and CodeLlama-13B seed 42/456 all produce exactly these 2 errors.
The root cause is deterministic: Python's \texttt{all()} raises \texttt{GeneratorExit} (a \texttt{BaseException} subclass) during generator short-circuit, recorded as \texttt{[ERROR]} despite the test passing.
However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
This confirms that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most initializations) rather than a hard data limitation: the representation supports perfect accuracy, though most LoRA initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
On this task, exception-only accuracy is \emph{signal-limited} rather than \emph{capacity-limited}: three architecture families spanning 1.5B to 13B converge on the same floor, while \texttt{no\_trace} shows monotonic scale dependence (67.3\% $\to$ 75.1\% $\to$ 76.5\%).

\paragraph{Tier hierarchy: practical implications.}
The two-tier structure (Tier~1 ${\geq}$99\%; Tier~2 = 85.6\%) has direct engineering implications for trace-augmented systems.
First, it implies a \emph{diminishing returns} principle: once a Tier~1 signal is available, adding more trace information provides no benefit and may actively degrade performance through attention dilution.
Second, the hierarchy suggests a fallback design: systems should attempt Tier~1 extraction (exception events) and only resort to Tier~2 signals (loop compression) when no exception is raised---though our results show that even Tier~2 alone substantially outperforms no-trace baselines (+10.50pp).
Third, the minimal token footprint of Tier~1 signals (${\sim}$200 tokens vs.\ ${\sim}$2{,}600 for VOTA) makes them viable for deployment in token-constrained settings (e.g., real-time CI pipelines, mobile inference).

\section{Introduction}

Execution traces---line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior---have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models \citep{chen2025tracepile,ding2024traced,wang2025dcsh,ni2024next}.
Yet a fundamental question remains: \emph{which components of an execution trace actually matter?}

\citet{wang2025dcsh} found that no single trace representation consistently outperforms others, but focused on generation-oriented tasks.
\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---is fundamentally different: it is fault detection, not generation.
Which trace components matter for this task type is unknown.

We present the first systematic study of what trace components drive verdict prediction.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program}, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components across four models spanning 1.5B to 13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B/1.5B-Instruct \citep{qwen2025coder}, CodeLlama-13B-Instruct \citep{roziere2024code}, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct \citep{deepseek2024coder}.

\textbf{Exception events alone achieve near-perfect verdict prediction across all four models: 99.83\% on Qwen-7B ($\pm$0.00, 3 seeds) and Qwen-1.5B, 99.89\% on CodeLlama-13B ($\pm$0.10, 3 seeds; one seed reaches 100\%), and 99.33\% on DeepSeek (2/3 seeds; 1 outlier at 91.09\%).}
VOTA degrades by 14.96pp on DeepSeek (confounded by tokenizer-driven truncation; 91.7\% of DeepSeek training samples were affected).
We approximately decompose the full-trace-to-VOTA gap into gradient dilution (${\sim}$26\%) and information overload (${\sim}$74\%), suggesting that irrelevant trace content is the primary bottleneck.
The novelty: (1)~adding trace information actively \emph{hurts}, (2)~we approximately decompose \emph{why} into a ${\sim}$26/74 split, and (3)~the cross-model gap is confounded by truncation (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Scale-invariant exception signal}: Exception events achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% across all four models (${\geq}$99.83\% on three of four; 1.5B--13B, three families), while \texttt{no\_trace} shows 9.19pp scale sensitivity (67.3--76.5\%); cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) yields 100\%, and a format-marker ablation confirms ${\sim}$91\% of the signal is semantic (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:nomarker}, \S\ref{sec:debugbench}).
\item \textbf{Information density decomposition}: The full-trace-to-VOTA gap approximately splits into gradient dilution (${\sim}$26\%) and information overload (${\sim}$74\%) (\S\ref{sec:density}).
\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy}: Tier~1 signals (exceptions, assertions) achieve ${\geq}$99\%; Tier~2 (loops) reaches 85.6\% (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

We presented the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction across four models (1.5B--13B, three architecture families).
Exception events alone achieve a near-perfect floor of 99.83\%+ across Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B ($\pm$0.00, 3 seeds), and CodeLlama-13B (99.89\%$\pm$0.10; one seed reaches 100\%), while \texttt{no\_trace} shows 9.19pp scale sensitivity (67.3--76.5\%).
Signal quality, not model capacity, determines verdict prediction performance.
The full-trace-to-VOTA gap approximately decomposes into gradient dilution (${\sim}$26\%) and information overload (${\sim}$74\%), and a format-marker ablation confirms that ${\sim}$91\% of the exception signal is semantic (SFT-learnable) rather than format-driven.
A cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench confirms generalization (\texttt{exception\_only}: 100\%, $N{=}426$).

The practical principle: for verdict prediction, extract the highest-specificity diagnostic signal and discard everything else.
Exception dominance is scale-invariant from 1.5B to 13B parameters and transfers across architecture families; future work should test whether this extends to additional programming languages, larger real-world codebases, and tasks beyond verdict prediction.
